content: Injected cholera vaccines are rarely used in modern medical practice, but they may still offer some benefits. It is important to evaluate their effectiveness in preventing cholera and related deaths, as well as their adverse effects, especially in comparison to newer oral cholera vaccines. The study aimed to assess the efficacy of killed whole-cell (KWC) cholera vaccines and other inactive subunit vaccines administered via injection. It also sought to evaluate the adverse effects associated with these vaccines. The research included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared injected cholera vaccines to placebo, control vaccines, or no intervention. These trials included participants of all ages, regardless of immune status or specific risk factors. The data collection process involved two independent authors who extracted information and assessed the methodological quality of the trials. The results were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and vaccine efficacy was calculated as a percentage using the formula: (1 RR) x 100%. The analysis included 16 trials with over one million participants, including adults, children, and infants. A total of 24 comparisons reported on vaccine efficacy in terms of cholera cases and/or deaths, while 11 comparisons evaluated adverse effects. Nine of these comparisons addressed both efficacy and adverse effects. The findings demonstrated that, compared to placebo, individuals who received the injected cholera vaccine had a significantly reduced risk of death from cholera (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.93; 837,442 participants). Additionally, the risk of contracting cholera at 12 months was reduced (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.65, random-effects model; 1,512,573 participants). This corresponds to a vaccine efficacy of 48% (95% CI 35% to 58%). The protection provided by the vaccine lasted for up to two years following a single dose and extended to three years with an annual booster. Adults and children over the age of five were protected for up to three years, while children under the age of five experienced protection for up to one year. Injected cholera vaccines were associated with a higher incidence of systemic and local adverse effects compared to placebo. However, these adverse effects were not severe or life-threatening. In conclusion, injected cholera vaccines are safe and more effective than is often recognized. They provide significant protection against cholera for up to two years with a single dose and up to three years with annual boosters. Despite their efficacy, these vaccines have largely been replaced by oral cholera vaccines in current medical practice.
